idiom_name: JVM pools (String.intern, Integer.valueOf caches, enums) plus @JvmInline value classes for handles
implementation_notes: Kotlin inherits the JVM's canonical pools - kotlin.text.intern() delegates to String.intern(), the Integer.valueOf caches are mandated by the language specification, and enum entries are canonical singletons - so identifier-like data is already shared. For custom intrinsic state the factory is a ConcurrentHashMap (or a WeakHashMap when entries must be collectable) with computeIfAbsent, the flyweight is a data class whose properties are all val, and @JvmInline value class can inline a single-field handle so only the underlying value travels at runtime. data class copy() and immutable collections keep the shared object genuinely read-only; var properties or mutable collections inside a flyweight defeat the pattern.
pitfalls: data class copy() and equals are shallow, and a MutableList property inside a shared flyweight is still mutable by every context; use read-only List, immutable collections or defensive copies.

String.intern() is a JVM-global native table: interning user-supplied or high-cardinality strings retains them for the process lifetime and can exhaust native memory. Keep interning to a small bounded vocabulary.
@JvmInline value classes are boxed when used as a nullable, generic or interface type, so a value-class handle silently allocates on those paths and the 'free handle' promise weakens.
A companion-object or top-level pool adds global initialization order to the picture: make sure the pool and the values it stores are initialized before they are published to other threads.
